articles.topicTitle: How to use this supplement library
articles.title: How to use this supplement library
articles.summary: Orientation for patients and practitioners using this clinic education library — how entries are framed and what they are not.

sections.heading: What this library is
sections.body: These pages are original clinic education notes inspired by common supplement and wellness questions that arise in osteopathic practice. They are written for both patients and practitioners. They are not a pharmacy training manual, product catalogue, or prescribing protocol.

sections.heading: How to read an entry
sections.body: Each page introduces topics in plain English, notes why they come up in MSK or recovery conversations, and lists safety caveats. Patients should treat them as background reading before speaking with a clinician. Practitioners should treat them as conversation prompts — not as clinical directives.

sections.heading: What we do not do here
sections.body: We do not endorse brands, quote retail scripts, or replace GP, pharmacist, or dietitian advice. Food supplements are not medicines and are not a substitute for assessment, rehab, or prescribed care.

caveats: Educational only for patients and practitioners.
Check medicines, pregnancy, and long-term conditions with a pharmacist or GP before starting supplements.

articles.title: Amino Acid
articles.summary: Clinic education notes on Amino Acid (also touching B Complex, Quercetin, Vitamin C) — for patients and practitioners, not a product recommendation.

sections.heading: In plain English
sections.body: Amino Acid often appears in conversations about diet quality, recovery, or general wellness. At Nguyen's Osteopathic Clinic we discuss supplements only as optional adjuncts after understanding load, sleep, and medical context — never as a stand-alone fix for back, neck, or joint pain.

sections.heading: Why it comes up in clinic
sections.body: People may ask about Amino Acid because of marketing claims, pharmacy advice, or something a friend suggested. Useful questions include: What problem are you hoping to change? Have bloods or a GP already reviewed diet? Are you on medicines that interact with concentrates?

sections.heading: Patient takeaway
sections.body: If you are curious about Amino Acid, bring the product label or a photo to your appointment or speak with a pharmacist. Food-first approaches and rehab loading usually matter more for musculoskeletal recovery than any single capsule.

sections.heading: Practitioner note
sections.body: Use this entry as a discussion scaffold around Amino Acid, B Complex, Quercetin, Vitamin C, Collagen. Confirm medical history, allergy, pregnancy/breastfeeding, and concurrent medicines before any patient self-supplements. Document advice boundaries clearly — osteopaths do not prescribe medicines.

caveats: Not a recommendation to buy or dose any product.
Evidence quality varies widely by ingredient and claim.
Seek urgent care for red-flag neurological or systemic symptoms.

articles.summary: Label-reading and formulation education (Glutamine) for patients and practitioners who want calmer conversations about ingredient lists.

sections.heading: Why labels look alarming
sections.body: Inactive ingredients (fillers, coatings, acidity regulators) sound chemical but often have ordinary food-tech roles. That does not make every product suitable — it means names alone are a poor scare test.

sections.heading: Focus for this sheet: Glutamine
sections.body: When reviewing labels that mention Glutamine, Ginseng, Muscle, ask what the active dose is, whether you need it, and whether your pharmacist is happy with interactions. Form (tablet, powder, oil) changes absorption and convenience more than marketing does.

sections.heading: Practitioner note
sections.body: Help patients prioritise actives and evidence over proprietary blends. Flag allergies (for example lactose, gelatine, or shellfish-derived ingredients) and renal or hepatic cautions where relevant.

caveats: Not a full pharmacopoeia.
When unsure, defer to a pharmacist.

sections.heading: Training load before powders
sections.body: Most sports discomfort improves with smarter volume, recovery days, sleep, and progressive strength. Products discussed in gym culture are optional extras after those basics are honest.

sections.heading: Notes on Multivitamin
sections.body: Multivitamin may appear in athlete conversations. We keep claims modest: understand the training goal, injury status, and medical history first. Hydration and protein from food cover many everyday needs.

sections.heading: Practitioner note
sections.body: Tie any supplement discussion to return-to-play criteria and tissue irritability. Avoid implying performance products heal tendons or discs.

caveats: Not anti-doping or sports-medicine clearance advice.
Check competition rules before using concentrated products.

faqs.question: Is this medical advice?
faqs.answer: No. It is dual-audience education for patients and practitioners at Nguyen's Osteopathic Clinic. Personal advice requires assessment.

faqs.question: Can practitioners use this in CPD reflection?
faqs.answer: Yes as a teaching prompt. It is not a formal CPD certificate or a substitute for regulated learning requirements.

articles.title: Vitamin A
articles.summary: Label-reading and formulation education (Vitamin A) for patients and practitioners who want calmer conversations about ingredient lists.

sections.heading: Why labels look alarming
sections.body: Inactive ingredients (fillers, coatings, acidity regulators) sound chemical but often have ordinary food-tech roles. That does not make every product suitable — it means names alone are a poor scare test.

sections.heading: Focus for this sheet: Vitamin A
sections.body: When reviewing labels that mention Vitamin A, Vitamin C, Vitamin D, Vitamin K, Chromium, ask what the active dose is, whether you need it, and whether your pharmacist is happy with interactions. Form (tablet, powder, oil) changes absorption and convenience more than marketing does.

sections.heading: Practitioner note
sections.body: Help patients prioritise actives and evidence over proprietary blends. Flag allergies (for example lactose, gelatine, or shellfish-derived ingredients) and renal or hepatic cautions where relevant.

caveats: Not a full pharmacopoeia.
When unsure, defer to a pharmacist.
